testlets.title: A weekend that went wrong
testlets.text: Last Saturday my friend Dima and I decided to go camping by a lake. The weather forecast said it would be sunny, so we didn't take warm clothes. We took the train in the morning and walked for two hours to find a good place. In the afternoon it was really hot and we swam in the lake. But in the evening it started to rain very hard. Our tent was old and the water came in. We couldn't sleep at all. At five in the morning we packed everything and walked back to the station. We were wet and tired, but now it is our favourite story to tell.

testlets.title: Swap shop
testlets.text: Every first Sunday of the month, the community centre on Green Street turns into a "swap shop". The idea is simple: people bring things they don't need any more — clothes, books, toys, small kitchen items — and take things that other people have brought. Nobody pays any money. The organiser, Vera Petrova, started the project three years ago after she moved house and found boxes of things she had never used. "I didn't want to throw them away," she says. "Someone else could use them." At first only a few neighbours came, but now about two hundred people visit each month. There is one rule: everything must be clean and work properly. Broken things go straight back home with their owners.

testlets.title: Learning to switch off
testlets.text:
When Anton Belov took a job at a software company, he was proud that he answered work messages within minutes, even late at night. After a year, however, he noticed that he was sleeping badly and getting irritated with his family over small things. "I was never really at home," he remembers. "My body was on the sofa, but my head was still at the office."

Anton decided to run a small experiment. For one month he turned off work notifications after seven in the evening and left his laptop in another room. The first week was uncomfortable: he kept checking his phone out of habit and worried that his manager would be annoyed. To his surprise, nobody complained. In fact, his manager admitted that she sent messages in the evening only because it was convenient for her, not because she expected an answer.

By the end of the month Anton was sleeping better, and he says his work has actually improved. "When I start in the morning, I have fresh ideas instead of yesterday's stress." He now encourages his team to agree on clear hours when they are not expected to reply.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Setting limits on work time helped Anton.

questions.prompt: What did Anton do during the experiment?
options: He stopped work notifications in the evening.

questions.prompt: Why did the manager send messages in the evening?
options: She worked in another time zone.

questions.prompt: "My head was still at the office" means Anton …
options: often worked late in the office

testlets.title: The town that banned cars (for a day)
testlets.text:
Three years ago the small town of Lindvik tried something its residents first thought was absurd: one Saturday a month, private cars were banned from the centre. Shop owners were the loudest critics. They were convinced that customers would simply drive to the shopping mall outside town and never come back.

The first car-free day did nothing to calm their fears. It rained, the free shuttle buses were late, and the streets looked empty. Several newspapers described the idea as "a well-meant failure". The town council, however, refused to give up. It added more buses, invited street musicians and allowed cafés to put tables in the road.

By the end of the first summer, the picture had changed. Families who had never walked through the old centre began to spend whole afternoons there, and many of the shop owners reported higher sales on car-free days than on normal Saturdays. Not everyone is convinced: some older residents still complain that they cannot reach the doctor's surgery easily, and the council has promised to provide a special transport service for them. Even so, a recent survey showed that two thirds of residents now want car-free days every weekend.

options: They had to close their shops.
They wanted to open on Sundays.

options: The idea was good but did not work.

The idea was expensive but popular.

questions.prompt: Which problem has not been fully solved?
options: access to the doctor's surgery for older people

testlets.title: In praise of boredom
testlets.text:
For most of us, boredom is something to be eliminated as quickly as possible. A queue, a delayed train or a dull meeting is enough to send a hand reaching for a phone. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that this reflex may be costing us more than we realise.

Their reasoning is that boredom is not simply an empty state but a signal: it tells us that our current activity is not meeting our needs and pushes us to look for something more meaningful. When that signal is instantly silenced by a stream of short videos, we lose the motivation it was meant to provide. Several small studies have found that people who were first given a deliberately tedious task — copying numbers from a phone book, for example — later produced more original ideas in a creativity test than those who went straight to the test.

The researchers are careful not to overstate their case. The studies are small, and chronic boredom, especially at work, is linked to stress and poor health rather than to inspiration. What they suggest is not that we should seek out boredom, but that we might tolerate short periods of it instead of treating every quiet moment as a problem to be solved. Leaving the phone in a pocket during a ten-minute wait, they argue, is a modest experiment that costs nothing — and might occasionally be where a good idea begins.

questions.prompt: What is the main argument of the text?
options: Boredom should be avoided at all costs.
Short periods of boredom may have benefits.

questions.prompt: According to the psychologists, what is the function of boredom?
options: It signals that we need something more meaningful.

testlets.title: The myth of the lone genius
testlets.text:
Popular history loves a lone genius: the inventor who, after years of solitary struggle, emerges with a world-changing machine. It is a satisfying story, with a clear hero and a dramatic moment of discovery. It is also, in most cases, misleading.

Historians of technology have long pointed out that major inventions tend to appear in several places at roughly the same time. The telephone, the light bulb and the jet engine all had multiple claimants, many of whom were working independently and were genuinely unaware of one another. This pattern is hard to explain if invention depends mainly on rare individual brilliance. It makes far more sense if we see inventors as people who assemble ideas, materials and techniques that are already circulating, at a moment when the surrounding conditions — markets, tools, scientific knowledge — finally make the assembly possible.

None of this means that individual talent is irrelevant. Someone still has to notice the opportunity, persist through failure and persuade investors to take a risk. But the emphasis matters. A culture that credits a single person with every breakthrough may underfund the less glamorous work on which breakthroughs depend: the maintenance of laboratories, the training of technicians, the sharing of data. If we want more inventions, the historians suggest, we would do better to invest in the crowded workshop than to wait for the solitary genius.

questions.prompt: What does the writer mainly challenge?
options: the idea that inventions come from isolated individuals

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention simultaneous inventions?
options: to show that some inventors copied others
as evidence that conditions, not just talent, drive invention

questions.prompt: What is the writer's position on individual talent?
options: It is the only real factor.

questions.prompt: What practical conclusion does the text suggest?
options: Fund the shared infrastructure of research.
Teach the history of technology in schools.
